extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in numerical solution of polynomial equations and series expansions (readers of The Mathematician / 19th-century mathematical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Numerical method for finding the complex (unreal) roots of trinomial equations by assuming a trigonometric (r(cos θ ± i sin θ)) form for roots, deriving equations for r and θ, and solving those (including parity and common-measure cases); includes related guidance on series expansions and elementary developments of algebra used in computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution for unreal roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume x = r (cos θ ± √-1 sin θ) (equation (2)) for seeking unreal roots of a trinomial ax^m + bx^k + c = 0, with m and n (exponents) prime to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this substitution to convert the polynomial equation into real and imaginary (or 'real and unreal') parts which yield two real equations in r and θ; this is the starting ansatz of the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equate real and imaginary parts to form two equations in r and θ
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute the trigonometric form into the trinomial and 'equate the real and unreal parts of the resulting equation separately to zero', obtaining equations such as ar^m cos mθ + br^k cos kθ + c = 0 and ar^m sin mθ + br^k sin kθ = 0 (as in (3),(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat r^m and r^n (or r^k) as unknowns and solve the two simultaneous equations to eliminate r and/or θ; follow the algebraic manipulations in the paper to derive explicit relations for r and θ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive sine-power equation for θ (equation (5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the two real equations to a single relation involving powers of sines: (—b)^m (sin nθ)^{...} (sin(m−n)θ)^{...} = a^n c^{...} (schematically equation (5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take logarithms of this sine-power equation to convert it to a form solvable by tables of logarithms and sines; this is the central scalar equation used to compute θ numerically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity handling to avoid sign ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: If m is even use the original equation (1) to avoid sign ambiguity; if n is even use equation (3); if both m and n are odd either may be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate form depending on parity of exponents to ensure correct sign handling when extracting roots or interpreting sine/cosine sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the rule of Double Position to find θ
rubrics_metrics.description: The author recommends the rule of Double Position (a numerical interpolation method) as 'best adapted to find the values of θ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Double Position (pairwise substitution and interpolation) combined with logarithms to refine θ to the desired precision; an example in the paper demonstrates successive interval subdivision and interpolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logarithms to linearize and handle coefficient magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Take logarithms of the sine-power equation (5) so that large or small coefficients a, b, c make little difference and computations can be carried out with common logarithmic and trigonometric tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logarithmic tables and trigonometric tables are used to evaluate expressions and to interpolate; the attainable number of correct figures is limited primarily by the precision of these tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign handling when a sine term is negative
rubrics_metrics.description: When the right-hand member is essentially negative, exactly one of the two sines (e.g., sin 3θ and sin 10θ in the example) must be negative; represent a negative sine by sin(α − 180°) to work with positive table entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace a negative sine term by the sine of (angle − 180°) before taking logarithms so that the logarithmic computation is consistent; this handling is key in the worked example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interval localization and iterative refinement for θ
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate θ in a specific interval (for example between 32° and 33°) by trial substitution into the log-equation, then refine by interpolation (ratios of differences) and successive substitution until desired precision is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example shows substituting endpoint values, computing the function values, and using proportional interpolation to get first an approximate minutes/seconds value, then iterating for finer accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute r from θ using derived formula
rubrics_metrics.description: After θ is found, determine r from an algebraic formula such as r^m = (c b sin mθ)/(a b sin nθ) or the formula given as (4) in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute r (and sign if relevant) using the appropriate formula; the example computes r and then returns pair(s) of unreal roots as r(cos θ ± i sin θ).

rubrics_metrics.name: When m and n have a common measure, reduce and proceed similarly
rubrics_metrics.description: If m and n share a common measure (gcd > 1), write the equation in reduced form with exponents h and k prime to each other (e.g., write ax^{hv} + bx^{kv} + c = 0), let z = x^v and apply the same trigonometric substitution and procedures to z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle the multiplicity of roots by generating multiple θ-valued solutions (2p, 2q, 2v values etc. as described) by varying an integer parameter through its range; follow the paper's prescription for even/odd v and sign cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour and precision considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The method 'admits of use being made of a table of logarithms' and 'the actual labour required to determine a single pair of unreal roots is nearly the same' regardless of the polynomial degree; 'the number of figures that can be obtained' is limited by common logarithmic and trigonometric tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the work to scale roughly proportionally to the degree when computing all roots; for high-precision work, the precision of available tables (or computational tools) is the limiting factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark for evaluating numerical root-finding methods: Horner's superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Horner's method is asserted to be superior for numerical solution of equations; improvements must be judged against Horner's practical efficiency and the number of decimal places attainable (examples: many students reached 50+ decimals; one reached 101+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing or assessing new methods, compare the method's achievable accuracy (decimal places) and computational labour against Horner's method as historical benchmark; the paper uses decimal attainment as a performance criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of indeterminate (conditional) coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a function may be developed as a series with coefficients to be determined (A0 + A1 x + A2 x^2 + ...), and determine coefficients by the condition that the assumed expansion be identically true (equate coefficients of like powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this method to carry out divisions or to produce series expansions: clear denominators, equate coefficients term-by-term, solve the resulting linear relations for the conditional coefficients (illustrated by dividing a^n − x^n by a − x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity-of-series theorem: equality of coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: If an equation A + B x + C x^2 + ... = A' + B' x + C' x^2 + ... is identical (true for all x), then the coefficients of the same powers of x must be equal (A = A', B = B', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this theorem as the foundational justification for the method of indeterminate coefficients and for comparing series expansions; the paper provides a proof by transposition to the same side and noting that nonzero coefficients would yield non-vanishing function terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's binomial theorem and its termination condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The development (1+z)^n = 1 + n z + n(n−1)/1·2 z^2 + ... holds generally; when n is a positive integer the series terminates and contains only n+1 terms, but when n is fractional or negative the series is infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the general factorial-like formula for coefficients; the k-th term is n(n−1)(n−2)...(n−k+1)/k! · z^k and vanishes beyond k = n when n is a positive integer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence criterion for binomial series
rubrics_metrics.description: When the series expansion is infinite, the ratio of consecutive terms approaches z as the index increases, so the series is divergent when |z| > 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict the use of the infinite binomial series to |z| < 1 (or otherwise use analytic continuation/other representations); the paper notes divergence for |z| > 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of a^x in ascending powers of x via logarithmic coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a^x = 1 + c1 x + c2 x^2 + c3 x^3 + ...; the coefficients are expressible in terms of natural logarithms of a, so that a^x = 1 + x ln a + x^2 (ln a)^2/2! + ... (equations (3') and following).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute coefficients by relating to Napierian (natural) logarithms and using the binomial theorem on a = 1 + b if convenient; when a = e the expansion simplifies to the exponential series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulus of logarithm systems and the Napierian base e
rubrics_metrics.description: The modulus m of a logarithmic system whose base is a equals 1/ln a; comparing expansions shows that e is the base for which the modulus equals 1, so e is the Napierian base from which exponential and logarithmic series are derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the natural logarithm base e for the canonical exponential and logarithm series; the paper derives relationships between bases, modulus, and series coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series expansions for inverse tangent, sine, and cosine and choice of angular unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop tan^{-1} x, sin x and cos x into power series by equating identities; coefficients are obtained from algebraic relations (examples: tan^{-1} x = x − x^3/3 + x^5/5 − ... and sin x = x − x^3/3! + x^5/5! − ... as derived). The paper discusses choosing an angular unit so expansions take a simple form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive trig-series coefficients via the same indeterminate-coefficient approach (use trigonometric identities to generate relations among coefficients); selecting an angular unit where sine-of-unit equals X simplifies constants (the author gives numerical angle-unit ~57°17'45").

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving coefficients via functional identities (general procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find coefficients in expansions (e.g., for log, exponential, trig functions), write the assumed series, substitute into known functional relations (addition formulas, double-angle, product-to-sum), equate coefficients term-by-term, and solve for coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This systematic approach is used throughout the paper for multiple functions (binomial, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric); the author advocates it as clearer and more uniform than other methods dependent on limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of algebraic identities for integer, negative, and fractional exponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas like (a^n − x^n)/(a − x) and the binomial expansion are shown to be valid when n is positive integer, negative integer, or fractional (with caveats such as x ≠ a when needed), by algebraic raising to powers and reducing to earlier cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extending identities to non-integer indices, proceed by raising assumed equations to appropriate integer powers and using limiting/analytic arguments as in the paper; verify special cases explicitly to ensure correctness.
